reading.body:
AI risk is being moved rather than priced: the market's answer to exposure carriers will not write is captives, mutual pools, surplus lines, and parametric cover tied to compute availability.

The ten mechanisms fall into three groups. Some retain risk inside the party that creates it, through hyperscaler single parent captives and startup mutual pools. Some push it into specialty markets, through surplus lines and reinsurance capacity caps. The rest try to make risk measurable and therefore tradeable, through parametric micro-insurance, catastrophe bonds, insured performance guarantees, and certification-linked discounts. Running alongside all of them are generative AI exclusion endorsements, which remove the risk from standard cover instead of transferring it.

Two instruments are indexed directly to compute. Parametric micro-insurance pays out on API and GPU availability, and catastrophe bonds hedge multi-day cloud shutdowns. That ties an insurance settlement to the same infrastructure the insured AI workload runs on, so a single prolonged outage can trigger claims across many holders at once. The captive mechanism matters for a different reason: when a hyperscaler self-insures what the commercial market declines, the cost of AI risk lands on its own balance sheet, competing for the same capital that funds compute and the buildings and power behind it.

The list is a taxonomy of instruments, not a measure of the risk. It names no carrier, no premium, no limit, no retention, and no date, and it gives no indication which of the ten are actually in force, at what scale, or whether they have paid out. Nothing here shows that AI losses are large, only that the market has built structures to hold them. Whether those structures are adequate is not answerable from this data.
